pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Salary History
Chandler received six merit increases during his time at The Post – all of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received merit increases in the following years: 1995, 1996, 1997 and 1998.

Explanation:
Chandler was paid a high salary at The Wall Street Journal – more than the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer at The Post at that time. Therefore, Chandler's starting salary at The Post was also higher than the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer at that time.

When he came to The Post, Chandler was given the title of Chief Economic Correspondent – reflecting the difficulty and importance of his work covering domestic economic policy, including tax policy.

Rajiv Chandrasekaran

Rajiv Chandrasekaran was paid substantially less than Hamilton on the 1996 and 1997 salary snapshots, similarly to Hamilton on the1998 salary snapshot and slightly more than Hamilton on the 1999 salary snapshot.

Chandrasekaran was paid substantially less than Mayer on the 1996 and 1997 salary snapshots, slightly less than Mayer on the 1998 salary snapshot and similarly to Mayer on the 1999 salary snapshot.

Experience and Education
Chandrasekaran came to The Post in the mid-1990s as a summer intern in Metro. He became a Two-Year Intern Reporter in Metro in 1994 and became a reporter in Metro in 1995. He became a reporter in Financial News in 1996, transferring to Foreign News as a reporter in 2000. Later in 2000 he became a foreign correspondent in the Jakarta Bureau, transferring to a similar position in the Cairo Bureau in 2002. He is now in Baghdad as a member of the Foreign Staff. Chandrasekaran is a graduate of Stanford University.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Chandrasekaran received approximately at 10 percent increase over his prior salary as a summer intern at The Post. His starting salary was substantially less than the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer at the time.

documents.title: Letter to Martha Hamilton enclosing check from maternity-leave arbitration settlement
documents.subject: Letter to Mrs. Martha Hamilton (Newsroom, Washington Post) enclosing Post check no. 950540 for $2,117.85 and explaining the Guild arbitration over sick leave during maternity leave
documents.notes: Typed letter, page 1 only; last line breaks off ('At that point, there') so the letter continues on a following page not in this batch. Handwritten '18' at top right (likely an exhibit/bates-like folio number) and a handwritten word above the address block, possibly 'spun' (unclear). No signature block visible on this page, so the sender is unknown.

pages.transcript:
[handwritten, top right corner: 18]
[handwritten word above address block, unclear: 'spun'?]

December 12, 1978

Mrs. Martha Hamilton
Newsroom
Washington Post

Dear Mrs. Hamilton:

Enclosed is Washington Post check number 950540 in the amount of $2,117.85.

Allow me to explain why we are giving you this check.

Several weeks ago there was an arbitration hearing scheduled with the Guild. The Guild's grievance was whether or not the language of the old, expired contract between The Post and the Guild required The Post to allow employees going on maternity leave to use some, or all, of their accrued sick leave while they were on maternity leave. The position of The Post was that the plain language of the contract did not require that, that was not the intent of the language, and, further, a consistent past practice had been not to grant sick leave to employees while they were on maternity leave. To put it another way, sick leave and maternity leave are two entirely different kinds of leave, and the language did not require that these two kinds of benefits could be used together.

documents.title: First-person career narrative statement, page 4 (paragraphs 11–13)
documents.subject: Martha Hamilton's first-person numbered narrative of her Post career: Weekly/convention-center series, Front Page award (1978), Tom Wilkinson and the Broyhill stories, Bob Woodward as Metro AME, NEH fellowship 1979, move to Financial under Frank Swoboda
documents.date: unknown (covers events 1978–1979; undated typescript, likely a grievance/arbitration statement)
documents.notes: Page 4 of a multi-page first-person statement; paragraphs 11–13, with the number '13' mistakenly used twice in the original. Content matches the résumé period in DOC-004 but is a different document form (narrative affidavit vs. CV). Mentions: Dominic Antonelli convention-center series, co-author Karlyn Barker, Bart Barnes, Len [downie?], John Warner's campaign managerRep. Joel T. pages.transcript:
11. I was side-tracked on the Weekly for many months, but ultimately came up with a project on the proposed convention center and then a series on developer Dominic Antonelli that got me on the front page. The series won the Front Page investigative reporting award for that year (1978). Downie, who was AME Metro, gave co-author Karlyn Barker and me bonuses for the series. My bonus was not incorporated into my base pay as a merit increase would have been. Downie told me he would take me off the Weekly. However, to open up a slot for me, he had to tell Bart Barnes that he was being sent back to Sports.

12. This apparently was hard for Len to do, so I stayed on the Weekly staff for several weeks until he managed to do so. I became a roving investigative reporter in Metro just as Len was leaving the Metro section. He was replaced as Metro AME by Tom Wilkinson. I spent many months on an investigation that included getting access to sealed court records, proving that former Rep. Joel T. Broyhill, a long-time friend of parking interests, had been set up in a no-show job by two parking magnates after his retirement, with benefits including a Rolls Royce Silver Cloud. Wilkinson said he didn't want to publish any of this because Broyhill, at the time, was John Warner's campaign manager and Wilkinson thought it would reflect unfairly on Warner.

13. In approximately 1979, Wilkinson was replaced as Metro AME by Bob Woodward. I didn't really have an assignment editor to whom I reported. I wasn't being used very well and had a hard time getting anyone interested in my projects. For instance, Woodward took interest in one project only after Bill Greider in Outlook expressed an interest in publishing it in Outlook. So I started to look for a different position. I was awarded a National Endowment For the Humanities fellowship to study economics in 1979 and was required to take leave without pay during the fellowship.

13. I began talks with Frank Swoboda, then day editor of Financial, about going to Financial. I went there on a temporary basis in October 1979 and quickly began doing front page work, writing about subjects including the national economy, budget issues, the environment and consumer debt.
